all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: Not recognized in the Vaikhānasa guru-paramparā. He favoured the Pāñcarātra mode of worship, contrasting with the Vaikhānasa system.

all_historical_figures.name: Āḻvārs
all_historical_figures.significance: Not recognized or worshipped in the Vaikhānasa tradition; their Tamil hymns are not sung.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrīnivāsa-makhin
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, the Lakṣmī-Viśiṣṭād-vaita-bhāṣya, establishing the distinct Vaikhānasa philosophical position.

all_historical_figures.name: Nātha-muni
all_historical_figures.significance: Leader who helped form the Śrī-vaiṣṇava group; the Vaikhānasa community predates him.

all_historical_figures.name: Yāmuna
all_historical_figures.significance: Leader of the Śrī-vaiṣṇava group; the Vaikhānasa community predates him.

all_historical_figures.name: Vikhanas
all_historical_figures.role: Founding sage of the Vaikhānasa tradition
all_historical_figures.significance: Believed to have written the Kalpa-sūtra (for householders) and taught the Daivika-sūtra (for iconic worship).

all_historical_figures.name: Marīci, Atri, Bhrgu, Kāśyapa
all_historical_figures.role: Four disciples of the sage Vikhanas
all_historical_figures.significance: They amplified the teachings of Vikhanas, and many Vaikhānasa texts are attributed to them.

all_historical_figures.name: Baudhāyana
all_historical_figures.role: Ancient smṛti-kāra and author of a Dharma-sūtra
all_historical_figures.significance: Acknowledged the Vedic authority of the Vaikhānasa scriptures.

all_historical_figures.name: Vallabha
all_historical_figures.significance: His commentary Subodhini suggests that the 'Vaidika' worship mentioned in the Bhāgavata-purāṇa refers to the Vaikhānasa tradition.
all_historical_figures.dates: 1479–1531 CE (not stated in text, but known)

all_historical_figures.name: Vīrarāghava
all_historical_figures.significance: Commented on the Bhāgavata-purāṇa, explaining the two approaches of 'veda' and 'tantra'.

all_historical_figures.name: Manu
all_historical_figures.significance: His Manu-smṛti counts the Vaikhānasa-sūtra among great authorities.

all_historical_figures.name: Gautama
all_historical_figures.significance: Accepts the authoritative character of the Vaikhānasa-sūtra.

all_historical_figures.name: Govindasvāmi
all_historical_figures.significance: Identified Vaikhānasa as a type of vānaprastha.

all_historical_figures.name: Haradatta
all_historical_figures.significance: Explained the Śrāmaṇaka method of kindling the sacred fire.

all_historical_figures.name: Kullūka-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned the Vaikhānasas had their own ideology and doctrine.

all_historical_figures.name: Kālidāsa
all_historical_figures.significance: His play 'Śākuntalam' refers to the Vaikhānasa as a life of austerity and vows.
all_historical_figures.dates: c. 4th-5th century CE (not stated in text)

all_historical_figures.name: Hārīta
all_historical_figures.significance: Provided details on the austere life of a Vaikhānasa hermit.

all_historical_figures.name: Yajñasvāmi
all_historical_figures.significance: Explained that 'śrāmaṇaka' means the Vaikhānasa-scripture.

all_historical_figures.name: Bodhāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Described the life of a Vaikhānasa hermit.

all_historical_figures.name: Nṛsimha-vājapeya-yāji
all_historical_figures.significance: Prepared an elaborate gloss on the Gṛhya and Dharma sections of the Vaikhānasa-sūtra, which provides the framework for the Vaikhānasa-āgama.

all_historical_figures.name: Vaidyanātha
all_historical_figures.significance: His Varṇāśramācāra-kāṇḍa classifies Kalpa-sūtras into two groups, 'earlier' and 'later'.

all_historical_figures.name: J. Gonda
all_historical_figures.significance: His analysis on the use of Vedic mantras in Vaikhānasa ritual texts is cited.

all_historical_figures.name: T. Gaṇapati Śāstri
all_historical_figures.significance: Published the Vaikhānasa text in Devanagari characters in 1913.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Edited a Telugu character edition of Vaikhānasa texts in 1915.

all_historical_figures.name: W. Caland
all_historical_figures.significance: Published an edition of Vaikhānasa Gṛhya and Dharma-sūtras in 1925 and 1927.

all_historical_figures.name: Dr. Eggers
all_historical_figures.significance: Published the Vaikhānasa-Dharma-sūtras in 1929.

all_historical_figures.name: R. Pārthasārathi Bhaṭṭācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Edited modern editions of Vaikhānasa texts published by TTD and Vaikhānasa-mahāmaṇḍali.

all_historical_figures.name: R. Śrīnivāsācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Edited the Srauta section of the Vaikhānasa-kalpa-sūtra in 1987.

all_historical_figures.name: Indra
all_historical_figures.significance: Frequently associated and identified with Viṣṇu. The Vaikhānasa sages were said to be dear to him.

all_historical_figures.name: Yāska
all_historical_figures.significance: His Nirukta is cited for the etymology of 'Viṣṇu' and the view of a single divinity appearing in multiple forms.

all_historical_figures.name: Aurṇavābha
all_historical_figures.significance: Interpreted Viṣṇu's three strides as the sun's movement at morning, midday, and evening.

all_historical_figures.name: Śākapūṇi
all_historical_figures.significance: Interpreted Viṣṇu's three strides as the sun's passage through earth, mid-region, and heaven.

all_historical_figures.name: Dīrghatama-aucathya
all_historical_figures.significance: Composer of the Ṛgveda hymn (1.155.1) which Vaikhānasas interpret as justifying iconic worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Sāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: His interpretation of 'arcata' as 'acquire well' is cited and rejected by the author in favor of the 'worship' interpretation.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaunaka
all_historical_figures.significance: His Ṛgvidhāna is cited to support the interpretation of 'arcata' as worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Vasiṣṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as an ancient authority for the worship of Viṣṇu.

all_historical_figures.name: Sanaka
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as an ancient authority for the worship of Viṣṇu.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrīnivāsa-makhin
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored 'Daśa-vidha-hetu-nirūpaṇam' and 'Tātparya-cintāmaṇi', which are cited as authoritative texts explaining the Vaikhānasa viewpoint.

all_historical_figures.name: Vikhanas
all_historical_figures.significance: The divine ancestor of the Vaikhānasa community and author of their foundational scripture, the Vaikhānasa-sūtra. Variously identified with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or a mind-born sage.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: The central object of worship for the Vaikhānasa community. He is also described as the ultimate source of their scriptural knowledge and in some accounts is identified with Vikhanas himself.

all_historical_figures.name: Brahmā
all_historical_figures.significance: Frequently identified with the sage Vikhanas, who received the divine knowledge from Viṣṇu and authored the sūtras.

all_historical_figures.name: Marīci, Bhṛgu, Atri, Kāśyapa
all_historical_figures.significance: The four hermit sons or disciples of Vikhanas who received the Vaikhānasa teachings and are credited with codifying them and founding the community. They are also considered authors of major Vaikhānasa texts.

all_historical_figures.name: Manu
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of the other sūtra-writers who accepted the contents and style of the Vaikhānasa-kalpa-sūtra.

all_historical_figures.name: Nara and Nārāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: In one origin story, they instructed the sage Vikhanas at Badarī to enlighten mankind about iconic worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu
all_historical_figures.significance: Listed alongside the main four sages as disciples of Vikhanas in the Naimiśa forest.

all_historical_figures.name: Nṛsimha-Vājapeya-yāji
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as the source for details on the worship of Vikhanas and the Viṣṇu-bali ceremony.

all_historical_figures.name: Hārīta
all_historical_figures.significance: His view is cited to distinguish Vaikhānasas from professional priests (devalakas).

all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānujācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as a guru whom the Vaikhānasas, unlike other Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas, do not recognize.

all_historical_figures.name: Āḻvārs
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as guides whose hymns (Prabandha) are not recited in Vaikhānasa worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaunaka
all_historical_figures.significance: Credited with the counsel to worship a beautiful icon of Viṣṇu to facilitate contemplation and attain Brahman.

all_historical_figures.name: Yudhiṣṭhira and Kṛṣṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Their dialogue in the Mahābhārata is cited to explain the Vaikhānasa and Pāñcarātra views on the forms of Godhead.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: The ultimate source of the Vaikhānasa doctrine, who taught it to the sage Vikhanas.

all_historical_figures.name: Vikhanas
all_historical_figures.significance: The first sage of the tradition, who received the Vaikhānasa-sūtra from Viṣṇu and transmitted it to his disciples. Considered a transformation of Vishnu's Vedic nature.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhṛgu
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the four main disciples of Vikhanas. He is credited with authoring the 'Adhikāras' (treatises on specific topics) like Kriyādhikāra and Prakīrṇādhikāra.

all_historical_figures.name: Marīci
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the four main disciples of Vikhanas. Credited with authoring the 'Samhitās' (collections) and the Vimānārcanā-kalpa, a key text cited for the tradition's origin.

all_historical_figures.name: Atri
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the four main disciples of Vikhanas. Credited with authoring the 'Tantras'.

all_historical_figures.name: Kāśyapa
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the four main disciples of Vikhanas. Credited with authoring the 'Kāṇḍas' (sections), including the Jñāna-kāṇḍa.

all_historical_figures.name: Nṛsiṁha-vājapeya-yājin
all_historical_figures.significance: A later commentator whose works, like the commentary on the Vaikhānasa-kalpa-Sūtra and Pratiṣṭhā-vidhi-darpaṇa, help explain the Vaikhānasa position.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrīnivāsa-makhin (Śrīnivāsa-dīkṣita)
all_historical_figures.significance: A prolific later writer and priest at the Tirumala temple. Authored works like Tātparya-cintāmaṇi and Vaikhānasa-mahima-mañjarī. Hailed as 'sarva-tantra-svatantra'.

all_historical_figures.name: Kātyāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of only two authors (along with Bodhāyana) whose extant kalpasūtras contain the Śulbasūtra section.

all_historical_figures.name: Bodhāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of only two authors (along with Kātyāyana) whose extant kalpasūtras contain the Śulbasūtra section.

all_historical_figures.name: Hārīta
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as a disciple of Bhṛgu whose views are frequently cited in commentarial literature.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaunaka
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of a 'Samhitā' belonging to the Vaikhānasa scripture, now lost but quoted by commentators.

all_historical_figures.name: Raghunātha Cakravarti-bhaṭṭacārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Editor of an early edition of Marīci's Vimānārcanā-kalpa.

all_historical_figures.name: Setu-mādhavācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Editor of an early edition of Marīci's Vimānārcanā-kalpa.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhattar Pārthasārathi Ācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Editor of Ānanda-saṁhitā (1924) with Sanskrit commentary.

all_historical_figures.name: Sundara-rāja
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Prayoga-vṛtti, a commentary on the Vaikhānasa-kalpa-sūtra.

all_historical_figures.name: Keśavācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: An early writer who prepared a gloss (vṛtti) on the Vedānta-sūtras and wrote Arcanā-navanīta on iconic worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhāskara-bhaṭṭacārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Disciple of Nṛsiṁha-Vājapeya-yāji, wrote commentaries on Daivika and Mānuṣika sūtras.

all_historical_figures.name: Ananta-nārāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Prepared a gloss on Vedānta-sūtras entitled Vārtikagrāhinī.

all_historical_figures.name: Kullūka-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Commented on Manu-smṛti (6.21) and acknowledged Vaikhānasa as both a 'dharma' and a 'darśana'.

all_historical_figures.name: Śrīnivāsa-makhin (or Śrīnivāsa-dīkṣita)
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored the 'Lakṣmi-Viśiṣṭādvaita-bhāṣya' on the Śārīraka-sūtras, crystallizing Vaikhānasa philosophy. Also wrote 'Vaikhānasa-mahima-mañjarī' and was known by the titles 'Sarva-tantra-svatantra' and 'Kavi-kula-tilaka'.

all_historical_figures.name: Raghupati-bhaṭṭācārya (better known as Vāsudeva, Vāsudevāpara-nāmā)
all_historical_figures.significance: Composed 'Mokṣopāya-pradīpikā', a significant and succinct presentation of Vaikhānasa philosophy, compiled from the works of Śrīnivāsa-makhin.

all_historical_figures.name: Divi Veṅkaṭanarasimhācārya
all_historical_figures.significance: Brought out an edition of 'Mokṣopāya-pradīpikā' in Telugu characters in 1948.

all_historical_figures.name: Vikhānas
all_historical_figures.significance: The foundational sage of the Vaikhānasa tradition to whom Viṣṇu is said to have communicated the Vaikhānasa-Śāstra.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhrgu
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the four foundational sages of the Vaikhānasa tradition. Quoted from his 'Vāsādhikāra'.

all_historical_figures.name: Nṛsiṁha-vājapeya-yājin
all_historical_figures.significance: Authored a commentary on the Vaikhānasa-sūtra, quoted for his explanation of saguṇa and nirguṇa contemplation.

all_historical_figures.name: Marīci
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the foundational Vaikhānasa sages whose work 'Vimānārcanā-kalpa' contains a detailed account of the philosophy, which is extensively summarized in the chapter.

all_historical_figures.name: Kāśyapa
all_historical_figures.significance: His 'Jñāna-kāṇḍa' is cited on the necessity of icon worship for ordinary people.

complete_timeline.event: Life of Rāmānuja, pre-eminent Śrī-vaiṣṇava ācārya.
complete_timeline.significance: His non-recognition by Vaikhānasas is a central marker of their distinct identity.

complete_timeline.event: Flourishing of Śrīnivāsa-makhin, a Vaikhānasa ācārya.
complete_timeline.significance: He authored a key Vaikhānasa philosophical text, demonstrating a well-developed, independent intellectual tradition concurrent with early Śrī-vaiṣṇavism.

complete_timeline.event: German indologists notice Vaikhānasa Kalpa-sūtra texts.
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the beginning of modern academic study of Vaikhānasa literature in the West.

complete_timeline.event: Publication of an edition of 'Mokṣopāya-pradīpikā' in grantha characters.
complete_timeline.significance: An early printed edition that served as the basis for a later Telugu version, indicating scholarly interest in the text in the early 20th century.

complete_timeline.event: T. Gaṇapati Śāstri publishes Vaikhānasa text in Devanagari.
complete_timeline.significance: An important step in making the primary texts available to a wider scholarly audience in India.

complete_timeline.event: W. Caland publishes editions of Vaikhānasa Gṛhya and Dharma-sūtras.
complete_timeline.significance: Key critical editions that became standard references for Western scholarship on the Vaikhānasas.
Continued the trend of critical European scholarship on Vaikhānasa texts.
Made the key philosophical text more accessible to a wider audience in the Vaikhānasa-bhagavaccāstra-granthamālā series.

complete_timeline.event: Life of Nātha-muni, early Śrī-vaiṣṇava ācārya.
complete_timeline.significance: The Vaikhānasa community is established as being an independent entity before the formation of the Śrī-vaiṣṇava group under his leadership.
The compilation of the foundational text of the Vaikhānasa school, which synthesized various aspects of Vedic ritual and domestic life (Śrauta, Gṛhya, Dharma, Śulba).

The development and codification of scriptures dealing with temple construction, idol worship, and philosophy, marking a major transformation in Hinduism. The Vaikhānasa Āgama represents the Vedic stream of this movement.

This historical trend led to a shift in religious focus from large, complex fire sacrifices (Śrauta) to more personal, domestic rituals (Gṛhya) and eventually to temple-based iconic worship, creating the need for Āgamic texts.
Provides a systematic account of the characteristic features and authority of the Vaikhānasa scriptures.
Further establishes the historical precedence of the Vaikhānasa tradition.

all_geographic_locations.place: Āndhra Pradesh, Karnāṭaka and Tamiḻ Nāḍu
all_geographic_locations.context: The three states in South India where the Vaikhānasa community is spread.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Defines the geographical extent of the community.

all_geographic_locations.place: Kerala or the coastal region of Karnāṭaka
all_geographic_locations.context: Regions in South India where the Vaikhānasa community is not found.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Further refines the specific geographic distribution.

all_geographic_locations.context: A long list of ancient Viṣṇu temples where worship is conducted according to Vaikhānasa prescriptions.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Demonstrates the historical importance and prevalence of the Vaikhānasa tradition in major South Indian shrines.

all_geographic_locations.context: Shrines associated with Rāmānuja and the Āḻvārs that continue to have Vaikhānasa priests.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Highlights the deep-rooted presence of the Vaikhānasa tradition, persisting even in centers of Śrī-vaiṣṇavism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as regions where various factions of Vedic Kalpa-sūtras are followed.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Provides a broader geographical context for the different Vedic schools in India.

all_geographic_locations.context: A 1915 edition of Vaikhānasa texts in Telugu characters was published here.

all_geographic_locations.place: Utrecht, New Delhi, Gottingen, Leipzig, Trivandrum
all_geographic_locations.context: Locations where key scholarly editions and studies of Vaikhānasa texts were published.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows the global and Indian centers of modern academic research on the Vaikhānasa tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: A sacred forest where Brahmā (as Vikhanas) performed austerities to recover lost divine knowledge, and where Vikhanas taught the foundational scriptures to his sage-disciples.
all_geographic_locations.significance: It serves as the mythological location for the origin and propagation of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra.

all_geographic_locations.context: A location where the sage Vikhanas performed austerities before traveling to the Himalayas.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A place of spiritual preparation for the sage Vikhanas.

all_geographic_locations.context: A site in the Himalayas where Vikhanas met the divine sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa and was instructed by them to spread the knowledge of iconic worship.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The location where the mission to disseminate Vaikhānasa teachings was divinely ordained.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the place where Bhagavan (Viṣṇu) instructed the sages.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A traditional, sacred forest location for the transmission of divine knowledge in Puranic literature.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as a possible identification for Śrīnivāsa, where the sage Atri worshipped Viṣṇu. Also, the location of Vaikhānasa families and the workplace of the commentator Śrīnivāsa-makhin.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major center for the Vaikhānasa tradition and the site of the famous Venkateswara Temple, where Vaikhānasa Āgama is practiced.

all_geographic_locations.context: The place where the sage Marīci worshipped Viṣṇu.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A mythological mountain associated with divine events in Hindu lore.

all_geographic_locations.context: The place where the sage Atri worshipped Viṣṇu, identified as possibly Tirumala.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A sacred site associated with an originating sage of the tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: The place where the sage Kāśyapa worshipped Viṣṇu.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A sacred site associated with an originating sage of the tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: The place where the sage Bhṛgu worshipped Viṣṇu.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A sacred site associated with an originating sage of the tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: The place of publication for the 1948 Telugu edition of 'Mokṣopāya-pradīpikā'.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A center for Vaikhānasa literary activity in the mid-20th century.

all_geographic_locations.context: The place where the 1905 grantha edition of 'Mokṣopāya-pradīpikā' was printed at the Lakṣmī-vilāsa Press.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A center of traditional printing and scholarship.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A community of temple-priests; followers of the sage Vikhanas; also synonymous with vānaprastha.
complete_terminology_index.context: The main subject of the chapter.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A major branch of Vaishnavism, particularly associated with Rāmānuja.
complete_terminology_index.context: Used as a point of contrast to define the Vaikhānasa tradition.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A division or school of the Kṛṣṇa-Yajurveda.
complete_terminology_index.context: The specific Vedic affiliation of the Vaikhānasa community.
The Vaikhānasas do not include Rāmānuja or the Āḻvārs in theirs.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Iconic worship; worship of a form.
complete_terminology_index.context: The central and superior mode of worship in the Vaikhānasa system.
An essential component of samūrtārcanā.
Equated with 'yajana' and considered a different, less superior approach than samūrtārcanā by Vaikhānasas.
The core concept of Vedic ritual, which Vaikhānasas see as fulfilled and surpassed by iconic worship.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Wisdom concerning Brahman; knowledge of the Absolute.
complete_terminology_index.context: Iconic worship is held to be more effective than even this.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A major Vaiṣṇava Āgamic tradition, favoured by Rāmānuja.
complete_terminology_index.context: Contrasted with the Vaikhānasa tradition, particularly in its relationship to the Vedas.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A type of Vedic ancillary text (Vedāṅga) dealing with rituals.
complete_terminology_index.context: The foundational scripture for the Vaikhānasa tradition.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A body of sectarian scriptures, especially concerning temple worship.
complete_terminology_index.context: Vaikhānasas represent a unique Āgama tradition that is fully integrated with the Vedic Kalpa-sūtra framework.
The term used to distinguish the Vedic approach from the Āgamic one in other traditions.
The Vaikhānasa term for their own scriptures, emphasizing their divine origin.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Aniconic worship; worship of the formless.
complete_terminology_index.context: Refers primarily to fire-rituals, contrasted with samūrtārcanā.
Synonymous with samūrtārcanā, considered the highest form of worship.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Pertaining to public Vedic sacrifices prescribed in the Śrutis.
complete_terminology_index.context: A major section of the Kalpa-sūtras, de-emphasized by Vaikhānasas due to its association with worldly desires.
A major section of the Kalpa-sūtras, stressed by Vaikhānasas.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The main, immovable icon in the sanctum.
complete_terminology_index.context: Corresponds to the gārhapatya sacrificial fire.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The movable icon used for daily worship (nityārcanā).
complete_terminology_index.context: Corresponds to the āhavanīya sacrificial fire.

complete_terminology_index.translation: The processional icon used for festivals.
complete_terminology_index.context: Corresponds to the dakṣiṇāgni sacrificial fire.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Forest-dweller; the third of the four stages of life (āśramas).
complete_terminology_index.context: The original lifestyle of the Vaikhānasa sages.
The characteristic sacrificial fire tended by Vaikhānasa hermits.
The Vaikhānasa Gṛhya-sūtras detail eighteen of these.
A sacrament unique to the Vaikhānasas.
A key Vedic equation underpinning the Vaikhānasa integration of sacrifice and Viṣṇu worship.
Another term for iconic worship, considered the best of three types.
The name of the priestly community.
The eighteen life-cycle rituals the Vaikhānasas undergo.
The twenty-six types of sacrifices performed by the community.
How Vaikhānasas style themselves, due to their acceptance of Vedic authority.
Refers to the Vaikhānasa-sūtra, their foundational scripture.
Refers to the tradition of iconic worship which they combine with Vedic rituals.
